USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the already-scheduled Trump-Xi G20 meeting to reopen talks without new U.S. concessions or a fresh tariff hike. Keep the January 1, 2019 List 3 step-up from 10% to 25% as unused leverage rather than firing it before Buenos Aires, and do not roll back Lists 1–3 or lock in purchase commitments until Beijing puts a concrete IP/tech-transfer offer on the table. A hold-and-talk posture is the right use of current leverage: further escalation now would poison the first leaders’ channel in a year, while preemptive rollback would give away the only clock China is watching.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high. Combined Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (Lists 1–2 at 25% plus List 3 at 10% from Sept 24), and China has matched on soy, autos, and aircraft and then added 5–10% on ~$60B (timeline 2018-07-06, 2018-08-23, 2018-09-24). That retaliation is biting the U.S. export channel: EXPCH fell from $10.86B in June to $8.65B in November (−20%), soy was ~$14B and roughly one-third of the U.S. crop, and farm-state prices and Brazil diversion were already documented through the summer and September. October market stress (VIX peak 24.98–25.23) and a stronger dollar (+4.4% on DTWEXBGS) plus CNY depreciation of ~9% (DEXCHUS 6.34 to 6.92) also blunt U.S. tariff pressure and raise input-cost/financial-volatility risk if List 3 jumps to 25% or a List 4 on remaining imports is launched. That is why the score sits above zero rather than in the opportunity zone. It is well short of +0.5 because the U.S. real economy is not yet in material drag: industrial production is still up (INDPRO 104.07), Michigan sentiment remains high at 97.5, CPI is contained, and the goods deficit, while wide, is not a recession signal. Midterm results (Democrats take the House) do not force a softer China line; contemporaneous reporting treated China hawks as bipartisan and tariff authority as presidential. Action stays near zero because the Nov 1 Trump-Xi call already reopened a leaders’ track for Argentina, official talks have been on hiatus, and Bloomberg/Reuters described drafting of possible terms rather than a deal. Escalating tariffs or entity-list action before that meeting would forfeit a cheap test of whether China will move on the Section 301 IP findings; conceding purchases or a partial rollback would be premature when Beijing has not tabled a matching structural offer and the May 19 “trade war on hold” joint statement collapsed within ten days.
key_factors: Section 301 already covers ~$250B; List 3 is scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019
China retaliation has hit soy/autos/aircraft; U.S. goods exports to China are down ~20% since June
U.S. domestic activity and sentiment remain solid, so the dispute is not yet a GDP-level threat
Yuan depreciation (~9%) and a stronger dollar are offsetting some U.S. tariff leverage
Nov 1 Trump-Xi call and planned G20 dinner reopen talks after a hiatus; no deal is on the table
Midterms flip the House but do not remove presidential tariff authority or bipartisan China-hawk consensus

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the existing retaliatory schedule and do not add new tariff or non-tariff measures before the Buenos Aires meeting. Use the 1 November Trump–Xi call and the agreed G20 dinner to reopen talks aimed at postponing the 1 January lift of List 3 from 10% to 25%, without locking in large purchase or structural concessions until Washington puts a matching, durable offer on the table. Prepare a bounded package (agricultural and energy purchases, process improvements on IP/JV practice) that can be tabled if the US is willing to freeze further escalation; do not repeat the May pattern of announcing purchases while the US still proceeds with Section 301.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. Combined US Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (List 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% from 24 September) and is scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 January 2019, with a further ~$267B tranche still threatened—enough to hit major export sectors and Made-in-China 2025 supply chains. Non-tariff pressure is real: the April ZTE denial order showed a single US licensing action can shut a national champion, August Entity List additions covered dozens of Chinese firms, and the 2019 NDAA bars federal procurement of Huawei/ZTE gear. Macro already shows the bite: industrial production slowed to 5.4% y/y by November, SA merchandise exports eased ~1.6% over the window, reserves fell ~$50bn, and USD/CNY moved from ~6.34 in mid-May to 6.92 on 7 November (~9%). That maps to the CHN +0.5 anchor (export hit, FX pressure, firm-level targeting) but not +1.0: IP is still expanding, reserves remain ~$3.08tn, the discount rate is unchanged at 2.9%, and authorities still have RRR/fiscal space. The US side is not collapsing either—US IP and sentiment remain firm, Fed funds are at 2.20%—so waiting Washington out is not costless. Action should not escalate: China has already matched $50B at 25% and put 5–10% on ~$60B more and is short of remaining US goods, while another Chinese move would make the leftover $267B and the January 25% hike more likely. Unilateral rollback or large purchase commitments are also wrong now: the 19 May joint statement (China to “significantly increase” purchases; Mnuchin “on hold”) collapsed ten days later when the White House proceeded with the $50B action, and Kudlow said as of early November the sides are “not on the cusp of a deal.” The midterm House flip does not create a US off-ramp—reporting on 7 November is that China policy is bipartisan and executive-driven. The correct stance is therefore negotiate at ~0: use G20 to seek a freeze and a sequenced bargain, keep current retaliation as leverage, and refuse to pay twice for a truce Washington has already broken once.
